:::{#def-subspace-sum}
#### Sum of subspaces

The **sum** of two subspaces $\mathcal{S}_1$ and $\mathcal{S}_2$ of $\reals^p$
(@def-subspace)
is the set of all sums of a vector from $\mathcal{S}_1$ and a vector from $\mathcal{S}_2$:

$$
\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2
\eqdef
\cb{\vecf{x}_1 + \vecf{x}_2 : \vecf{x}_1 \in \mathcal{S}_1,\ \vecf{x}_2 \in \mathcal{S}_2}.
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-subspace-sum}
#### Two lines sum to a plane

Let $\mathcal{S}_1 = \operatorname{span}\cb{(1, 0, 0)}$
and $\mathcal{S}_2 = \operatorname{span}\cb{(0, 1, 0)}$,
two lines in $\reals^3$.
A vector of $\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2$ has the form
$a\,(1, 0, 0) + b\,(0, 1, 0) = (a, b, 0)$,
and $a$ and $b$ can be any numbers,
so $\mathcal{S}_1 + \mathcal{S}_2 = \cb{(a, b, 0) : a, b \in \reals}$,
the plane $z = 0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-sum-not-union}
#### The sum is not the union

For the two lines in @exm-subspace-sum,
the union $\mathcal{S}_1 \cup \mathcal{S}_2$
contains $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$
but not their sum $(1, 1, 0)$:
every multiple of $(1, 0, 0)$ has second entry $0$,
and every multiple of $(0, 1, 0)$ has first entry $0$.
So the union is not closed under addition and is not a subspace,
while the sum, the whole plane $z = 0$, is.

:::
